content.text: {"answers": [{"question_id": "Q1", "question": "How do you currently keep track of which supplies are running low — for example, do you rely on visual checks, a written list, a spreadsheet, or any kind of app or tool?", "answer": "The household uses a household inventory list to track stock levels. Physical counts are performed and recorded there. Reorder thresholds for each item are also stored in this list, so stock levels can be compared against those thresholds systematically rather than relying purely on visual judgment."}, {"question_id": "Q2", "question": "At what point do you decide a supply needs to be reordered — is there a specific quantity remaining, a number of days' worth left, or is it more of a judgment call each time?", "answer": "There is a defined household reorder threshold for each item. When the counted stock falls below that threshold, the item is proposed for replenishment. If stock is still above the threshold, the item is left off the order. It is not a judgment call — the threshold drives the decision."}, {"question_id": "Q3", "question": "Where and how do you place the order when a supply is low — for instance, through an online store, a subscription service, or by going to a physical shop?", "answer": "Orders are placed through an online shop. Once the basket is reviewed and confirmed against product and spending constraints, the order is placed and an order confirmation is saved for reference. The specific online shop or whether a subscription is used is not specified further."}, {"question_id": "Q4", "question": "Can you list the main types of supplies you manage, and roughly how many distinct items are involved in this process?", "answer": "The specific types of childcare supplies and the exact number of distinct items are not specified in the available information. What is noted is that items must come from an approved product list, and any substitutions require parent confirmation."}, {"question_id": "Q5", "question": "When a delivery arrives, do you do anything beyond putting items away — such as checking that the quantities match the order or noting the new stock level somewhere?", "answer": "Yes. When a delivery arrives, the receiving caregiver first checks the delivery against the saved order record to verify quantities match. If there is a discrepancy, that is treated as an exception. After verification, items are stored and the household inventory count is updated to reflect the new stock levels."}, {"question_id": "Q6", "question": "Do you check stock levels on a regular schedule, such as weekly, or do you only look when you happen to notice something is running out?", "answer": "Stock is checked on a regular schedule — twice a week in this household. Counting and preparing the shopping list takes about ten minutes each time. It is not reactive; checks happen proactively on that fixed cadence."}]}
